section.title: Final Greetings
section.sectionRationale: The letter closes as warmly as it began. Having warned against deceivers, the elder sets down his pen mid-thought, longing to come in person so that joy may be full, and passes on greetings from a sister church. The close returns the reader to love and joy after the stern middle.
section.thesis: The elder has much more to say but prefers to speak face to face so that shared joy may be complete, and he sends greetings from the children of the readers' elect sister, closing the letter in the warmth of the family of God.
section.frameNote: Two beats: the wish to come and speak face to face for full joy; greetings from the elect sister's children.

units.label: Face to face
units.note: that our joy may be complete

verses.text: I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with paper and ink. Instead, I hope to come and speak with you face to face, so that our {{chara|joy}} may be complete.
The children of your {{eklekte|elect}} sister send you greetings.

chara.gloss: Joy, gladness, delight. The elder writes so that joy may be complete or made full, the same aim John names in his other letters. Christian joy is not solitary; it is completed in fellowship, in the shared life of God's people gathered face to face.

eklekte.gloss: Chosen, elect, selected by God. The readers were greeted in verse 1 as the chosen lady; now greetings come from the children of their elect sister. The word frames the whole letter, binding two communities together as families chosen by the same gracious God.

basic.context: The letter ends on a warm, personal note. The elder says he has much more to write but would rather come and talk in person, because seeing one another completes their joy. Then he passes on greetings from another church, the children of the readers' elect sister. After the sharp warning, the close returns to love and family.
basic.hermeneutics: These are ordinary closing remarks of an ancient letter, but they carry real weight. The preference for face-to-face over paper and ink shows that the truth is meant to be lived in personal fellowship, not only read. And the note about complete joy reveals the goal behind even the stern warning: the full, shared gladness of God's people.
basic.originalLanguages: The elder writes so that joy, chara, may be made full, an aim he names elsewhere too. The greeting comes from the children of the readers' elect, eklekte, sister, the same word used of the chosen lady in verse 1, framing the letter and binding the two communities as one family.
basic.typology: There is no formal type here, yet the longing to be present face to face quietly anticipates the great hope of Scripture: seeing God face to face, when joy will at last be complete in His presence.
basic.christ: The joy the elder seeks is the joy Jesus prayed His people would share fully, the joy He gives that no one can take away. The whole letter has guarded the truth about Christ; now it points to the fellowship and joy that truth secures, all of it grounded in Him.
basic.god: God is a God of joy who gathers His people into one family across distances, chosen sisters and their children. He means His truth to be enjoyed in fellowship, and He is bringing His people toward the day of complete joy in His presence.
basic.crossReferences: 3 John ends almost identically, preferring to speak face to face. 1 John says its aim is that joy may be complete. Jesus in John's Gospel speaks of His joy made full in His people.
basic.oneStory: The letter closes with the hope of presence and full joy, which is where the whole Bible story is going: God's chosen family gathered, the truth kept, and joy completed face to face. The stern warning served this end, that nothing would rob God's people of the shared gladness He is bringing them into.

context.literary:
The two verses are a brief closing, but they are built to answer the opening. The letter began by addressing the chosen lady and her children, and it ends with the children of her elect sister. The first verse spoke of the elder's love, and this last paragraph speaks of his longing. In between, the letter has moved through joy at the readers' faithfulness, an appeal to love, and a stern warning, and now it settles back into the personal register of the beginning. The warm frame holds the hard centre, which is exactly how the elder wants the warning to be heard.

The contrast of media is the heart of verse 12. The writer has 'many things' to say, but he will not say them 'with paper and ink.' He sets the written word, which is what the reader now holds, against speech 'face to face,' which in the Greek is literally 'mouth to mouth,' a detail the BSB footnote records. The sentence ends with the purpose, 'so that our joy may be complete,' and so the whole letter, which began with truth and love, closes on joy.

Almost every phrase is shared with the closing of 3 John, which has 'I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with pen and ink,' followed by the same hope to speak face to face. The near repetition shows that the two letters belong together, and also that the elder had a settled way of closing. What is different is notable. Third John ends with a blessing of peace and with greetings to friends by name, while 2 John ends at verse 13 with no farewell wish at all. The brief stop gives the letter a feeling of suspended warmth, as though the elder were already getting up to go.
context.historical:
Writing in the first century was costly and slow. A letter like this was copied onto a sheet of papyrus with a reed pen and ink, and it travelled by hand with a trusted person, since there was no postal service for private letters. The carrier often added what the letter left unsaid. For that reason many letters were brief on purpose, and a short letter on a single papyrus sheet was no embarrassment. The elder's apology, that he has much more to say but will not put it on 'paper and ink,' reflects both the limits of the medium and the preference for presence that all ancient letter writers shared.

Paul expresses the same longing for presence in many places. He tells the Thessalonians that his desire to see them face to face was intense, 1 Thessalonians 2:17, and he prays night and day to be able to see them, 1 Thessalonians 3:10. He tells the Romans that he longs to see them, Romans 1:11, and Timothy that he longs to see him so that he may be filled with joy, 2 Timothy 1:4. Such wishes were conventional, but they were also deeply meant, and the early church's whole life depended on visits that carried news, teaching and encouragement.

The closing greeting reflects how the churches were connected. Believers in one city sent greetings to those in another, as in Romans 16:16, 1 Peter 5:13 and Colossians 4:15. Greetings were not formalities but the means by which scattered congregations remembered that they belonged to one body. The sister's children who send greetings in verse 13 are the elder's own circle or another household known to the readers, and their message is a reminder that the lady's household is not alone in its stand for the truth. In a season when false teachers were moving from house to house, the knowledge that a sister community was standing firm was a real encouragement.
context.canonical:
The closing ties 2 John to the rest of the Johannine writings. First John states its own purpose as 'We write these things so that our joy may be complete,' 1 John 1:4, and 2 John 12 uses the same verb for completion. In the Gospel, Jesus says to His disciples, 'I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete,' John 15:11, and again in John 16:24 and 17:13. John the Baptist also says of himself that his joy is complete, John 3:29. The notion of complete joy runs through John's whole witness as one of the aims of the gospel.

The preference for presence has deep roots in Scripture. The LORD spoke to Moses face to face as a man speaks to his friend, Exodus 33:11, and Numbers 12:8 makes this the mark of Moses' unique closeness to God. The hope of seeing the Lord face to face grows throughout the Bible, and in the New Testament it becomes the believer's destiny: 'Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face,' 1 Corinthians 13:12, and 'They will see His face,' Revelation 22:4.

The final greeting from the elect sister's children places the letter in the wider family of New Testament churches. The language of household and sisterhood belongs with Paul's picture of believers as members of God's household, Ephesians 2:19, and with the Jerusalem above that is our mother, Galatians 4:26. The elder's last word is not a doctrine but a family greeting, and the canon sees nothing odd in this, since the church from the beginning was a family before it was an institution.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The elder wants to leave his readers with warmth and with hope. After a letter that has contained a stern command, he needs them to understand that his severity springs from affection and from an expectation of meeting them. The hope of a visit is partly a promise: he will come, they will talk, and what is only sketched here will be filled out.

He also wants them to understand the limits of a letter. Writing can state a principle, but it cannot hear a question, read a face or share a meal. Some things in the situation of the church, perhaps the names and details of the false teachers, perhaps the harder questions about how to respond, are better settled in person. The elder is not putting the letter beneath the spoken word in authority. He is making a pastoral point about what kind of communication a living church needs.

Finally he intends the greeting of verse 13 to bind the two communities. The readers are not an isolated house under siege. They belong to a family that has other members, who send their love. A church that knows it is not alone is better able to stand for the truth, and that is the last thing the elder wants his readers to take away.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These verses describe. They tell us what the elder wishes to do and what the sister's children have asked him to pass on. There is no command in them. It would be a mistake to read verse 12 as a rule that Christians must never write about spiritual things, or that a letter is always inferior to a visit. The text is a personal comment on one man's circumstances.

What the verses model is a way of caring for a church. They show a leader who values presence, who is willing to travel to meet people, and who links the aim of his ministry to the joy of those he serves. They show churches who send their greetings across the distance. These are examples that a congregation can follow, in the use of letters, visits and conversations as well as the new media of our time. The key principle is that digital or written contact should lead to fellowship in person where that is possible, and not replace it.

The verses also give a gentle caution to any church that relies wholly on distant teaching and communication. Written or broadcast truth is real, and the elder has just written it. But joy is completed in meeting.

debates.question: Why does the elder say he will not write more?

views.label: The limits of papyrus and the demands of tact
views.case: The letter was a short one, written on a single sheet, and the carrier could say what was not committed to ink. Sensitive matters, such as the names of teachers or the handling of a particular visitor, were better handled orally. The elder says as much when he writes of the 'many things' he still has to say.

views.label: A stock formula that also expresses real longing
views.case: The nearly identical wording in 3 John 13-14 suggests a formula that he used to close short notes, in line with ancient letters that spoke of the writer's hope of a visit. It does not follow that the wish was insincere, since Paul uses similar language with real feeling, 1 Thessalonians 2:17.

views.label: A pastoral conviction that presence matters
views.case: The elder pairs the hope of speaking mouth to mouth with the aim of complete joy. He sees that some things that teaching and encouragement can do are done only in company, and that is why he does not treat writing as a substitute.

debates.bearing: The views are not rivals. A short letter, a stock formula and a real conviction can all be present at once. The reading that best serves the passage notices that the wish is genuine and that it ties the letter's purpose to joy shared in person.

debates.question: Is the hope to visit a real plan or a conventional closing?

views.label: A real intention connected to the crisis
views.case: The warning of verses 7 to 11 needs follow-up, and the elder expects that a visit will allow him to do what a letter cannot. He also describes himself as one who comes, in contrast to the false teachers who come with a different teaching, and a visit from the elder himself would be the surest way to restore confidence.

views.label: A conventional note of presence
views.case: Ancient letters often closed with a hope to visit as a way of keeping the relationship alive, and the repetition in 3 John suggests that the elder used the phrase more than once. On this reading the hope is sincere but not tied to a specific date or plan.

debates.bearing: The text offers no date, so the difference remains a matter of emphasis. Either way, the verse shows a leader who thinks of his readers as people he wants to be with, and who ties his plans to God's will, as Paul does in Romans 15:32 and James teaches in James 4:15.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for 'paper' in verse 12 is chartes, a sheet of papyrus, and it occurs only here in the New Testament. The word for ink is melan, literally 'the black stuff,' as in 2 Corinthians 3:3, where Paul says the Corinthians are a letter written 'not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God.' The matching line in 3 John 13 speaks of ink and a reed pen, melanos kai kalamou. Together they paint a picture of the writer's desk: the sheet, the pen and the pot.

The elder says he did not 'wish' to write more, ouk eboulethen, an aorist tense, which is how Greek letter writers often stated their present decision. The BSB renders it softly as 'would prefer not.' The verb elpizo, 'I hope,' is the ordinary word for a confident expectation and is used throughout the New Testament of both ordinary plans and the great hope of the gospel. Paul uses it of his plans to visit in Romans 15:24, and writes of trusting that he will come soon in Philippians 2:24. The elder's hope is held under God's will, which is the attitude of Romans 15:32.

The phrase 'face to face' is literally stoma pros stoma, 'mouth to mouth,' a Greek idiom for direct conversation. It says that the elder wants to speak, not to be seen, and the same phrase is used in 3 John 14. The Hebrew of Numbers 12:8 has the same picture of the LORD speaking with Moses 'mouth to mouth,' which the BSB renders 'face to face.' The word for 'speak,' lalesai, is a general word of conversation.

The expression 'so that our joy may be complete' uses the perfect passive participle with the verb 'to be,' pepleromene e, a form that describes a state that has been brought about and stands. The verb pleroo, 'fill,' is John's own word for the completion of joy in John 15:11, 16:24 and 1 John 1:4. A few manuscripts read 'your joy' in place of 'our joy,' but the sense is similar either way, since the joy that comes from meeting is shared.

In verse 13 the verb aspazetai, 'greets,' is singular, and it takes the singular pronoun se, 'you,' addressed to the lady, with 'the children' as subject. The text then says 'of your elect sister,' tes adelphes sou tes eklektes. The BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts add 'Amen' at the end, a common scribal closing, and the earliest text ends at the greeting. The absence of a farewell blessing is striking in comparison with 3 John 14, where peace is wished on the reader.

typology.type: Face to face with God, from Moses to the new creation
typology.fulfillment: The LORD spoke to Moses face to face as a man speaks to a friend, Exodus 33:11, and Numbers 12:8 sets this above the way He spoke to other prophets. It was a privilege given to one man for a time. In Christ it is extended to all who belong to Him: in the new creation 'they will see His face,' Revelation 22:4, and 'then we shall see face to face,' 1 Corinthians 13:12. The elder's hope of speaking mouth to mouth is a small, earthly taste of that promise. The type falls short because Moses could not see God's face and live, Exodus 33:20, while believers will see Him fully.

The Law was written on tablets of stone, and Paul says that the Corinthians are a letter from Christ, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, on tablets of human hearts, 2 Corinthians 3:3. The elder's refusal to rely only on paper and ink fits the same pattern: the real letter that God writes is the life of the church. In Christ, the Spirit writes the truth within, Jeremiah 31:33, and the church is a living message. The pattern does not make Scripture unnecessary, since the elder has written a letter and so has Paul.

Isaiah 54:1 speaks of a barren woman who will have more children than the one who has a husband, and Paul reads the Jerusalem above as 'our mother,' Galatians 4:26. The lady and her children in the letter, with the sister and her children, resemble this picture of the church as a mother with a large family. The text does not say the elder had Isaiah in mind, so this is a pattern and not a prediction. The correspondence is that the people of God are one family spread across many households, and it falls short if pressed, since the church in the letter is a local fellowship and not the whole of Zion.

study.christ:
The close leads to Christ by the incarnation that the letter has defended. In verse 7 the elder insisted that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. In verse 12 he says that he would rather come and speak face to face than write. The two ideas are close neighbours. A God who values flesh and blood presence has done so by sending His Son, who made His dwelling among us, John 1:14. The Word did not simply send a letter from heaven. He came. John begins his first letter with the apostles who heard, saw and touched the Word of life so that their joy may be complete, 1 John 1:1-4, and the joy of the church is tied from the beginning to a person who could be seen and heard.

It leads to Christ in the joy He gives. 'I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete,' John 15:11. The elder's longing for complete joy is not his own invention but an echo of the Lord's. Jesus also promised, 'I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy,' John 16:22, and He prayed that His disciples might have His joy fulfilled within them, John 17:13. His own joy was real: He endured the cross 'for the joy set before Him,' Hebrews 12:2. The joy that the elder seeks is a share in the joy of the Son.

It leads to Christ in the promise of His return. He said, 'I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am,' John 14:3. The elder's hope of coming to his readers is a small picture of that larger hope, and Christians are people who live by the expectation of an even greater meeting.

It leads to Christ by the shape of the family. The sister's children who greet the readers are members of one household, and Paul says that believers are 'members of God's household,' Ephesians 2:19, in the one who has broken down the barriers between people. The family is the Son's work. And when two or three gather in His name, He is with them, Matthew 18:20, which is why even a small house church could expect to meet Him.

There is a restraint to keep. The passage is not an allegory for Christ's second coming, and the elder's hope of a visit should not be forced into a prediction. The links that matter rest on the incarnation, on Christ's own words about joy, and on His presence among His gathered people.
study.god:
The closing shows God as the source of joy. The elder's aim is not simply to teach but to see joy made complete, and he ties it to fellowship. This is how the Bible speaks of God. He is the one in whose presence there is fullness of joy, Psalm 16:11, and He rejoices over His people with singing, Zephaniah 3:17. The God of these verses is not a stern lawgiver who happens to permit gladness. He is a joyful God who gathers a joyful people.

He is a God who comes. From the garden, where the LORD God walked in the cool of the day, Genesis 3:8, to the tent where He spoke to Moses face to face, Exodus 33:11, to the Word made flesh, John 1:14, God's way has been to be present with His people and not merely to send messages. The elder's wish to be present mirrors the character of the God he serves. The promise at the end of the Bible is that God Himself will be with His people as their God, Revelation 21:3.

He is a God who works through ordinary means. The elder uses a letter, a messenger, a hope of travel and the greetings of friends. God does not bypass these but uses them to carry the truth and nurture joy. At the same time the elder holds his plans humbly, as Paul does when he says that he hopes to come to the Romans 'by God's will,' Romans 15:32. God rules the plans of His servants, and the servant trusts Him with the details.

He is a God who makes a family. The final greeting is from the children of an elect sister to the children of an elect lady, and 'elect' is God's word. He is the one who chooses and gathers households across distances, and who makes strangers members of His household, Ephesians 2:19. The unity of the church is His work.

For worship, the passage invites the church to gather. Joy is completed in company, and the people of God are most themselves when they meet. It teaches believers to value letters, calls and messages, but to seek fellowship in person and to take their meeting as a foretaste of the day when they will see His face.

crossReferences.note: The closing of the companion letter says almost word for word what verse 12 says, with pen and ink and the hope to speak face to face, and then adds a wish of peace and greetings by name. Reading them together shows the elder's habit of closing and highlights how brief the ending of 2 John is.

The first letter says that the apostles heard, saw and touched the Word of life, and writes so that joy may be complete. The same aim and the same verb of completion lie behind verse 12, and the passage shows that this joy rests on the incarnate Word.

Jesus says that He has spoken to His disciples so that His joy may be in them and their joy complete. It is the source of the elder's phrase and shows that the joy he wants for his readers is the joy of the Lord Himself.

Jesus tells His disciples that their grief will turn to joy, that He will see them again and no one will take their joy away, and that they should ask so that their joy may be complete. The passage links complete joy to meeting the Lord.

Paul speaks of his intense desire to see the Thessalonians face to face and his night and day prayer for the opportunity. It is a close parallel to the elder's hope and shows how normal and deeply felt this longing was for the apostolic circle.

Paul asks for prayer that by God's will he may come to the Romans with joy and be refreshed with them. It shows the same pairing of hope to visit, joy and submission to God's will that stands behind verse 12.

Paul says the Corinthians are a letter from Christ, written not with ink but with the Spirit on human hearts. It reflects the same sense that the church is God's living message, which is why the elder prefers presence to paper and ink.

Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. The verse puts the elder's small hope of a face to face meeting in the setting of the greater hope of seeing the Lord, and explains why such meetings are precious.

The LORD spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. It is the Old Testament root of the phrase and shows that face to face speech is a mark of friendship with God, a privilege now offered to the whole church.

Peter sends greetings from the church in Babylon, chosen together with his readers, and from Mark. It is a close parallel to the greeting from the elect sister's children and shows how the apostolic letters closed with greetings that bound churches together.

Paul sends greetings to the brothers in Laodicea and to Nympha and the church that meets at her house. It shows the usual practice of greeting between congregations and the central role of households in the life of the early church.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with presence. God walks in the garden with the man and woman, Genesis 3:8, and the first tragedy is that they hide from Him. The long story that follows is the story of how God comes back to be with His people: in the tent of meeting, where He spoke to Moses face to face, Exodus 33:11, in the tabernacle and temple, in the prophets' promises that He would dwell among His people, and finally in the Word made flesh who made His dwelling among us, John 1:14. The elder's wish to come and speak to his readers is a small echo of this great movement toward presence.

The story also has a thread of joy. God made the world to be enjoyed and a people to enjoy Him, and the sin of Genesis 3 brought sorrow. The prophets promised a day when the redeemed would enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy, Isaiah 35:10. Jesus entered the story and spoke of joy that would be complete and could not be taken away, John 15:11 and 16:22. The elder's aim that the joy of his readers should be complete is a line from the same story, set in a letter to a small house church.

It is also a story of a family. God called a man, made him a nation and then called a people from every nation, so that strangers became fellow citizens and members of God's household, Ephesians 2:19. The two sisters and their children of this letter are a picture of that family in the first century, two households, each chosen, each loved, each sending greetings across the miles.

And the story is still on its way. The elder writes in a world of paper and ink and hopes to see his friends. The Bible promises a day when God Himself will be with His people, when He will wipe away every tear, Revelation 21:3-4, and when they will see His face, Revelation 22:4. The partial meeting of the letter's close is a promise of that greater one. Until then the church holds the truth, keeps love and meets when it can, and that is the story the little letter ends on: joy, made complete, in the presence of those who belong to the family of God.

sermon.title: The Danger of Deception
sermon.why: Begg's message on 2 John 1:7-13 carries through to the letter's close, treating the elder's wish to come face to face for complete joy and the greetings from the sister church. A clear, orthodox handling that reaches this final movement.

quiz.q: Why does the elder prefer not to write everything with paper and ink?

options.text: He hopes to come and speak face to face so that their joy may be complete.
options.note: Verse 12 names his preference for personal presence and its aim, full joy.

options.text: He had run out of things to say.
options.note: He says the opposite; he has many things to write.

options.text: He distrusted letters as a way to teach.
options.note: He values presence more highly, but he still writes; the point is completeness of joy, not distrust.

options.text: He wanted to save the cost of writing materials.
options.note: Paper and ink are mentioned, but the reason given is joy made complete in person, not thrift.

quiz.q: What does the elder say completes their joy?

options.text: Being together face to face in fellowship.
options.note: Verse 12 ties complete joy to personal presence among God's people.

options.text: Winning the argument against the deceivers.
options.note: The warning matters, but the joy named here is that of fellowship, not victory in dispute.

options.text: Receiving a reply letter from the readers.
options.note: He desires communion, but specifically face-to-face presence, not merely a written reply.

options.text: Being left alone to write in peace.
options.note: He longs for presence with others, not solitude.

quiz.q: Who sends greetings at the end of the letter?

options.text: The children of the readers' elect sister.
options.note: Verse 13 conveys greetings from the elect sister's children, likely a sister church.
The greeting comes from the family of God, not from the false teachers.
The greeting is from the elect sister's children, not from scribes.
The greeting is from fellow believers, the elect sister's children, not merchants.

quiz.q: How does the word elect, used of the sister, connect to the rest of the letter?

options.text: It echoes the chosen lady of verse 1, framing the letter and binding both communities as God's chosen family.
options.note: The same word opens and closes the letter, tying the two together in God's choosing.

options.text: It is an unrelated coincidence of wording.
options.note: The repetition deliberately frames the letter with the language of election.

options.text: It shows the sister church was superior to the readers.
options.note: Both are called elect equally; there is no ranking.

options.text: It refers only to a person's social rank.
options.note: The word points to God's gracious choosing, not to social standing.

questions: The elder longed to be present rather than only to write. Where in your own life is face-to-face fellowship being crowded out, and how might you recover it?
His aim was that their joy would be complete. Do you think of Christian joy as something completed together rather than alone, and how could you pursue that this week?
After a stern warning, the letter ends in warmth and family greetings. How does it help you to see that guarding the truth and deep affection belong together?
The close quietly points toward seeing God face to face. How does that final hope of complete joy in His presence shape the way you live and love now?

translationNotes.note: 'Face to face' renders a Greek idiom, literally 'mouth to mouth', as the BSB footnote notes, stressing direct personal presence.
'That our joy may be complete' can also be read 'that your joy may be complete'; manuscripts vary, and the sense of shared, full joy holds either way.
Some manuscripts add 'Amen' at the close, as the BSB footnote notes; the BSB text omits it.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 2 John 1:12-13. verse 12 'mouth to mouth' idiom and verse 13 'Amen' variant noted per the BSB footnotes.
